etymology: From Old French piler, from Latin pila, a pier or column. Hebrew distinguishes two things the English word merges: 'ammūd is a structural column that stands and bears weight, from 'āmad, to stand; matstsebah is a standing stone set up as a memorial or witness. The distinction matters, since Scripture commends the one and repeatedly condemns the other when it is raised to a false god.
biblical_def: A pillar in Scripture is something that stands and makes others stand, and God takes the figure to Himself in the wilderness: “And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night” (Exo 13:21) — a column of God's own presence, giving shade in the day and light in the dark, and moving so that Israel's marching orders were visible to every man in the camp. Against that stands the pillar a soul becomes when it refuses to move: “But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt” (Gen 19:26) — a monument to a heart that had left Sodom in body only, and the Lord Jesus made her a warning to His own disciples in one sentence: remember Lot's wife. The word is then applied to the church, and the metaphor assigns it a definite office: “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15). A pillar does not generate what it holds; it displays and upholds it, which is exactly the church's relation to truth she did not invent. Men may be pillars too, and Paul names three without flattery: “James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars” (Gal 2:9). And the promise to the overcomer takes the figure into permanence: “Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out” (Rev 3:12) — spoken to the church at Philadelphia in a region whose cities were shaken by earthquakes and whose people repeatedly fled them.
webster_summary: A column or upright support; a standing stone set up as a memorial; and in Scripture the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel, the pillar of salt Lot's wife became, the church as the pillar and ground of the truth, and the pillar the overcomer is made in God's temple.
webster_full: PILLAR, n. 1. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated, used to support or adorn a building.
2. A supporter; that which sustains or upholds; that on which some superstructure rests.
3. A monument raised to commemorate a person or event; a standing stone.
4. In Hebrew, from a root signifying to stand; that which stands and causes to stand.
5. In Scripture, a pillar of a cloud, a pillar of fire. Exod. 13. The pillar and ground of the truth. 1 Tim. 3.
corruption_summary: The church is made the source of truth rather than its support, so that her pronouncements are treated as generating what they were given to uphold; and at the other extreme her office as pillar is denied altogether in favour of a purely private religion.
corruption_paragraphs: 1Ti 3:15 is the classic proof text of Roman claims for the magisterium: because the church is the pillar and ground of the truth, it is argued that her teaching office is the truth's foundation and guarantor, so that Scripture depends on the church for its authority and the church may add to it. The metaphor itself refutes the inference. A pillar does not produce the building it holds, and nothing is truer for being displayed on a column. The church's office is to hold up, exhibit, and guard what she has received — the faith once delivered unto the saints, which she may not add to and may not amend. The Bereans were commended for testing an apostle's preaching by the Scriptures, which would be impossible if the teaching body were the standard rather than the servant of the standard.

The opposite corruption discards the office entirely. Where Christianity is treated as a private matter between the individual and God, the visible church becomes optional, and the truth is left with no appointed upholder in the world. Scripture assumes otherwise everywhere: elders are charged to hold fast the faithful word, to convince the gainsayers, and to commit what they have heard to faithful men who shall be able to teach others also. The principle to recover is the exact relation the figure sets: Scripture is the truth, the church is the pillar, and a pillar that carries nothing has failed as surely as one that claims to have made the roof. The promise of Rev 3:12 is the personal form of the same thing — the overcomer himself made a fixture in God's temple, who shall go no more out.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ammūd is a structural column, from 'āmad, to stand; matstsebah is a standing stone or memorial pillar, condemned when raised to false gods. Greek stulos is a pillar or column.

Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing stone set up as memorial or witness; Jacob's pillar at Bethel (Gen 28:18), and the images Israel was commanded to break down.
Hebrew n'tsīb (H5333) — a pillar or garrison, that which is set up; the word for the pillar of salt in Gen 19:26.
Greek stulos (G4769) — a pillar or column; the pillar and ground of the truth (1Ti 3:15), and the pillar in the temple of God (Rev 3:12).
Greek hedraiōma (G1477) — a stay, support, or ground; paired with stulos in 1Ti 3:15 to describe the church's office.

Of the church's office: the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth (1Ti 3:15).
Of the overcomer's permanence: him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God (Rev 3:12).

etymology: From Old French chambre, from Latin camera, a vaulted room. The Hebrew cheder is an inner room — the innermost, most private part of a house, reached only by passing through the outer rooms — while 'aliyyâh is the upper chamber built on the flat roof, the cool and quiet room reserved for a guest. Greek tameion is a storeroom or inner chamber, and it is the word the Lord Jesus uses for the place of private prayer, rendered closet in the King James.
biblical_def: The chamber in Scripture is the private room, and it is the appointed place of two things: hospitality and prayer. The Shunammite woman's provision for Elisha is one of the most concrete acts of kindness in the Old Testament, and it is furnished item by item: “Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither” (2Ki 4:10). A bed, a table, a stool, a lamp — hospitality in Scripture is specific rather than sentimental. The Lord Jesus makes the inner room the test of whether prayer is addressed to God or to an audience: “But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly” (Mat 6:6) — the shut door being the one thing that makes hypocrisy pointless. Isaiah uses the chamber for shelter under judgment, in a call full of tenderness: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast” (Isa 26:20) — language that deliberately recalls the households shut in behind blood on the night of the Passover. And the psalmist uses the bridegroom's chamber for the sun's rising, in a figure of unspent gladness: “Which is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race” (Psa 19:5).
webster_summary: An apartment in a house, particularly an inner or upper room; a place of retirement, lodging, or private prayer — whence the prophet's chamber, the closet with the door shut, and the chambers into which God calls His people till the indignation be past.
webster_full: CHAMBER, n. 1. An apartment in an upper story, or in a story above the lower floor of a dwelling house.
2. Any retired room; a private apartment which a person occupies.
3. A hall of justice or of a legislative body; as, the chamber of the senate.
4. In Hebrew, an inner room, the most private part of the house; also an upper room built upon the roof.
5. In Scripture, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father. Matt. 6. Enter thou into thy chambers. Isaiah 26.
corruption_summary: Private devotion is either abandoned in favour of a wholly public and performed religion, or absolutised into a purely private faith that owes nothing to the assembly — Scripture commanding the closet and the congregation together.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 6:6 is aimed at religion conducted for spectators, and the target has not changed — only the platform has. The hypocrites of the Sermon on the Mount prayed at street corners to be seen of men; the modern equivalent is devotion curated for an audience, where the act and its display are simultaneous. The Lord's prescription is a room and a shut door, and its logic is that a reward from men and a reward from the Father are mutually exclusive: they have their reward is the bleakest sentence in the passage. Nothing in the command forbids public prayer — He Himself prayed aloud before crowds, and the Acts church prayed together constantly. What it forbids is prayer whose real audience is horizontal, and the closet is prescribed as the cure because it removes the audience entirely.

The corruption in the other direction takes the closet as a warrant for a private religion which needs no church — a faith of personal devotion alone, accountable to nobody. The same Lord who commanded the shut door commanded a table, a baptism, and a body of elders, and rebuked the neglect of assembling as a bad habit. Isa 26:20 is instructive here, for the chambers are entered by a people — come, my people — households sheltering together as at the Passover. The principle to recover is that Scripture knows nothing of a choice between private and corporate religion: the man who prays only in public is a hypocrite, and the man who prays only in private is a deserter, and the same chapter of the same Bible names both.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheder is an inner or innermost room; 'aliyyâh is the upper chamber on the roof, the guest room. Greek tameion is an inner chamber or storeroom, rendered closet, and huperōon is the upper room of Acts.
roots_lines: Hebrew cheder (H2315) — an inner room, the most private part of a dwelling; the chambers of Isa 26:20 and the bridegroom's chamber of Psa 19:5.
Hebrew 'aliyyâh (H5944) — an upper chamber built on the flat roof; the prophet's chamber prepared by the Shunammite (2Ki 4:10).
Greek tameion (G5009) — an inner chamber or storeroom; enter into thy closet (Mat 6:6), a room with a door that shuts.
Greek huperōon (G5253) — an upper room; the place of the Last Supper and of the disciples' waiting in Act 1:13.
Hebrew chuppah — a canopy or bridal chamber; the covering under which the marriage was celebrated, echoed in Psa 19:5.
usage: Of hospitality made concrete: let us make a little chamber... a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick (2Ki 4:10).
Of secret prayer: enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret (Mat 6:6).
Of shelter under judgment: enter thou into thy chambers... until the indignation be overpast (Isa 26:20).

etymology: From Old English bedd. Hebrew mishkāb is from shākab, to lie down, and covers both the place of sleep and, by a natural euphemism, the marriage bed; mittâh is a couch or litter. Greek koitē is likewise the marriage bed and gives the English coitus, which is why Heb 13:4 uses it for the conjugal relation itself rather than the furniture.
biblical_def: The bed in Scripture is where a man is most alone and least defended, and the Bible visits him there with both comfort and warning. It is the place where grief is loudest, and David does not conceal it: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Psa 6:6). It is the place a man discovers he cannot escape God, and the psalm says so with a shudder and then with relief: “If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there” (Psa 139:8). The marriage bed is declared honourable and guarded in the same sentence, so that the two halves cannot be separated: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge” (Heb 13:4) — Scripture holding both that the conjugal relation is pure and good in itself, and that God will judge those who take it outside its covenant. The bed is also the picture of an inadequate refuge, in one of Isaiah's most memorable images of false security: “For the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it: and the covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it” (Isa 28:20) — every refuge but God is a bed too short and a blanket too small. And the bed becomes the token of a cure that leaves nothing to argue with, when the man who was carried in carries his own bed home: “I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house” (Mar 2:11).
webster_summary: That on which a person lies or sleeps; the marriage bed, declared honourable and undefiled; the place of sickness, grief, and sloth; and in Isaiah the bed too short for a man to stretch upon, the figure of every false refuge.
webster_full: BED, n. 1. Something to sleep or repose on; a couch; anything on which a person lies or reclines.
2. Lodging; a convenient place for sleep. To make the bed, is to put it in order.
3. Marriage; matrimonial connection. Marriage is honorable and the bed undefiled. Heb. 13.
4. A plat or level piece of ground in a garden, usually raised; as a bed of herbs.
5. In Scripture, I water my couch with my tears. Psalm 6. The bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it. Isaiah 28.
corruption_summary: The marriage bed is either treated as shameful by an ascetic instinct that regards the body with suspicion, or detached from covenant altogether, so that the honour Hebrews grants it is claimed while the judgment attached to it in the same verse is ignored.
corruption_paragraphs: Heb 13:4 makes two statements in one breath, and both halves are needed. The first — marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled — rebukes the long ascetic tradition that has treated the conjugal relation as a concession to weakness and celibacy as inherently holier. Scripture gives no such ranking. Marriage is instituted before the fall, its physical union is commanded and not merely permitted, and Paul forbids husbands and wives to defraud one another. The teaching that forbids marriage he names among doctrines of devils. The body is not a lower part of a man to be tolerated; it is the part God formed first and the part He will raise.

The second half is where the modern corruption falls: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge. The honour of the bed is claimed without the boundary that constitutes it, so that the goodness of sexual union is affirmed and the covenant that makes it good is treated as an optional cultural form. On Scripture's account the two cannot be separated, because what is honoured is not an act but a one-flesh covenant — therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife. Outside that, the same act is named as a sin against a man's own body and placed under judgment. The principle to recover is the whole verse: nothing about the marriage bed needs apology, and nothing about it survives being taken outside the covenant — and the bed that is not God's appointed refuge will always prove, like Isaiah's, too short (Isa 28:20).

etymology: From Old English topp. The Hebrew is simply rō'sh, head — the top of a mountain, a tower, or a staff being its head. The word therefore carries no separate idea of eminence; what is at the top is at the head, which is why the same noun means chief, beginning, and summit. Scripture's use of the word is dominated by a single contrast: tops men build to reach heaven, and tops God lets down to reach earth.
biblical_def: Two towers stand at the head of Scripture's use of this word, and they are opposites. At Babel men propose to reach God by construction, and the motive is stated without disguise: “Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth” (Gen 11:4) — a name of their own and a security of their own, and the LORD came down to see the tower, which is the narrative's quiet comment on how far up it reached. Then at Bethel a fugitive with a stone for a pillow is shown the real connection, and he does not build it: “And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Gen 28:12). The top that reaches heaven is let down, not raised, and the Lord Jesus later identifies Himself as that ladder. The word also marks the place of intercession, where the battle below is decided by the hands lifted above: Moses says, “to morrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand” (Exo 17:9), and Amalek prevails whenever those hands come down. And at the end of a long life the same word appears in a posture of worship that Hebrews singles out: “By faith Jacob, when he was a dying, blessed both the sons of Joseph; and worshipped, leaning upon the top of his staff” (Heb 11:21) — the man who once wrestled now leaning, and blessing, and worshipping.
webster_summary: The highest part or summit of anything; the head of a mountain, tower, or staff; and in Scripture the tower top of Babel that men raised toward heaven, the ladder top let down at Bethel, the hill top of Moses' intercession, and the staff top on which dying Jacob worshipped.
webster_full: TOP, n. 1. The highest part of any thing; the upper end, edge or extremity.
2. The surface; the upper side; as the top of the ground.
3. The highest place or rank; as, he is at the top of his profession.
4. In Hebrew, the head; the same word serving for the top of a mountain, the head of a man, and the chief of a company.
5. In Scripture, a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven. Gen. 11. A ladder... the top of it reached to heaven. Gen. 28.
corruption_summary: Religion is treated as ascent — a tower of technique, experience, or moral achievement by which men climb toward God — when Scripture consistently presents the connection as let down from above and never built from below.
corruption_paragraphs: Babel is the archetype of every religion of ascent, and its features are exactly reproduced wherever men attempt God by construction: a project undertaken together, a technique adequate to the goal, and above all a name secured for the builders. Let us make us a name is the engine of the thing. The instinct survives in more respectable forms — ladders of mystical experience, programmes of self-improvement offered as sanctification, and any scheme in which a man ascends to God by intensity of effort. Scripture's judgment on the whole enterprise is delivered in a single deadpan line: the LORD came down to see the city and the tower. From the top of the highest structure men can raise, God still has to stoop to look.

The counter-image is Bethel, and its details are all deliberate. Jacob is running for his life, has nothing, deserves nothing, and is asleep. The ladder is set up — he did not raise it — and the traffic on it begins at the top. The Lord Jesus claims the vision as a description of Himself: ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. The principle to recover is that Christianity is not a religion of ascent but of descent and reception: no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven. Every gospel that requires a man to climb has, whatever its vocabulary, gone back to Shinar; and the posture Scripture commends at the end is not a summit reached but an old man leaning on the top of his staff, worshipping (Heb 11:21).
roots_summary: Hebrew rō'sh is head, and hence top or summit, whether of a mountain, a tower, or a staff. Greek akron is an extremity or tip, and koruphē a summit; the ladder of Bethel is sullām in Hebrew, a word found only there.
roots_lines: Hebrew rō'sh (H7218) — head; and so the top of a mountain, tower, or staff, and the chief of a company.
Hebrew sullām (H5551) — a ladder or stairway; a word occurring only at Gen 28:12, probably from sālal, to cast up a highway.
Hebrew Babel — from bālal, to confound; the name of the tower city becoming the memorial of the confusion of tongues (Gen 11:9).
Greek akron (G206) — an extremity, tip, or top; leaning upon the top of his staff (Heb 11:21).
Greek kataba'inō / anaba'inō — to descend and to ascend; the angels ascending and descending (Joh 1:51), where Christ applies Jacob's ladder to Himself.
usage: Of the tower men build upward: a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name (Gen 11:4).
Of the ladder let down: a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven (Gen 28:12).
Of intercession above the battle: I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand (Exo 17:9).

etymology: From Old English brādu, from brād, broad. Hebrew rōchab is from rāchab, to be wide or spacious — the same root that gives the name Rehoboth, room, which Isaac gave to the well nobody contested. Greek platos gives the English plateau and platitude, and is one of the four dimensions Paul asks that the saints may comprehend.
biblical_def: Breadth in Scripture is a measurement word which becomes a theological one, because the things God measures and the things He cannot be measured by are both instructive. Zechariah sees a man going out with a measuring line and asks his errand: “Then said I, Whither goest thou? And he said unto me, To measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof, and what is the length thereof” (Zec 2:2) — and the surveyor is stopped, because the city God intends will be inhabited as towns without walls for the multitude of men in it, too large for the line. The heavenly city at the end is measured and found to be a perfect cube: “And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal” (Rev 21:16) — the same proportions as the holy of holies, the whole city being the most holy place. The tabernacle furniture is likewise given in exact dimensions, because obedience in worship is specific: “they shall make an ark of shittim wood: two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof” (Exo 25:10). And Paul takes the vocabulary of measurement and applies it to the one thing that defeats it, praying that the saints “may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height” (Eph 3:18) — and then, in the next verse, that they may know the love of Christ which passeth knowledge. The dimensions are named precisely in order to say that this is the one thing no reed will span.
webster_summary: The measure or extent of anything from side to side; width; one of the four dimensions Paul prays the saints may comprehend, and a measure of the heavenly city whose length and breadth and height are equal.
webster_full: BREADTH, n. 1. The measure or extent of any plain surface from side to side; width.
2. In building and mensuration, the shorter of the two horizontal dimensions of a surface.
3. In Hebrew, from a root signifying to be wide or roomy; whence Rehoboth, room, and enlargement as a figure of deliverance.
4. In Scripture, the breadth, and length, and depth, and height. Eph. 3.
5. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal. Rev. 21.
corruption_summary: The love of God is either reduced to a sentiment small enough to be fully mapped and mastered, or made so indefinite that it is emptied of the definite content Scripture gives it in the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: Eph 3:18 has a structure that is easily missed and is the answer to both errors. Paul asks that the saints may comprehend the breadth, length, depth, and height — a word of real apprehension, not vagueness — and then that they may know a love which passeth knowledge. Both are prayed for together. The first corruption drops the second half: the love of God becomes a manageable quantity, a doctrine mastered and filed, or worse a mild benevolence entirely proportionate to human expectation. Anyone who has genuinely reckoned with the cross knows the dimensions run off the page — that God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us, is not a proposition one finishes.

The opposite corruption drops the first half, treating divine love as so far beyond understanding that nothing definite may be said of it — which in practice becomes a warrant for saying whatever one likes, since a love with no shape cannot contradict anything. Scripture's love has a very definite shape: hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us. It is measured at Calvary, and it is because it is measured there that it can be preached, trusted, and appealed to. The principle to recover is the balance of the prayer itself: the love of Christ has dimensions the saints are meant to explore together — with all saints, since no one comprehends it alone — and it will not be exhausted, which is why the city at the end is measured (Rev 21:16) and is still large enough to hold every nation.
roots_summary: Hebrew rōchab is breadth or width, from rāchab, to be wide or spacious, whence Rehoboth and the figure of enlargement. Greek platos is breadth, one of the four dimensions of Eph 3:18.
roots_lines: Hebrew rōchab (H7341) — breadth, width; used constantly in the tabernacle and temple measurements.
Hebrew rāchab (H7337) — to be or grow wide, to enlarge; thou hast enlarged me when I was in distress (Psa 4:1).
Hebrew R'chōbōth — room or broad places; the well Isaac named because for it there was no strife (Gen 26:22).
Greek platos (G4114) — breadth; the breadth, and length, and depth, and height (Eph 3:18), and the measure of the city (Rev 21:16).
Greek katalambano (G2638) — to seize, grasp, comprehend; the verb in Eph 3:18, of a real apprehension of what nevertheless passeth knowledge.
usage: Of the city too large for the line: to measure Jerusalem, to see what is the breadth thereof (Zec 2:2).
Of the exactness of worship: two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth (Exo 25:10).
Of the dimensions of Christ's love: may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height (Eph 3:18).

pos: n. and v. (rendering Hebrew middâh and 'ēphâh, Greek metron)
etymology: From Old French mesure, from Latin mensura. Hebrew middâh is a measure or extent, from mādad, to measure; the commercial measures — ephah for dry goods, hin and bath for liquid — are separately named, and the law repeatedly requires that they be just. Greek metron gives English metre, and in the New Testament it is used chiefly of the measure God apportions and the measure a man applies to others.
biblical_def: Measure in Scripture is used in three ways, and each is weighty. First, God is the measurer of creation, and Isaiah's rhetorical question is designed to reduce the reader to silence: “Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?” (Isa 40:12) — the seas held in a cupped palm, the sky spanned between thumb and little finger. Second, the measure a man uses on others is the measure God will use on him, and the Lord Jesus states it as a fixed principle in both directions. In judgment: “For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again” (Mat 7:2). And in generosity, where the return is deliberately extravagant: “Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom” (Luk 6:38) — the picture of a grain merchant packing a container past any honest requirement. Third, measure describes what God gives, and here the one exception is Christ Himself: “For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God: for God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him” (Joh 3:34). Every servant receives a portion; the Son receives without measure. And the goal set for the church is stated in the same vocabulary: till we all come unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ (Eph 4:13).
webster_summary: The extent or dimension of a thing ascertained by a standard; a vessel or rule by which extent is ascertained; the just measures required by the law; and in Scripture the measure a man metes to others, and the Spirit given to Christ without measure.
webster_full: MEASURE, n. 1. The whole extent or dimensions of a thing, including length, breadth and thickness.
2. That by which extent or dimension is ascertained, either length, breadth, thickness, capacity, or amount.
3. A limited or definite quantity; a certain portion or proportion; as a measure of corn.
4. Moderation; just degree; as, to observe measure in all things.
5. In Scripture, with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again. Matt. 7. God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him. John 3.
corruption_summary: The promise of good measure running over is converted into a technique of investment, so that giving becomes a means of getting; and the warning that we are measured as we measure is quietly exempted from application to ourselves.
corruption_paragraphs: Luk 6:38 is the standard proof text of transactional giving: give in order that it shall be given unto you, with the return specified as pressed down and running over. Read in context the verse says something quite different. It stands at the close of a paragraph about loving enemies, lending without hoping for return, being merciful as your Father is merciful, and not judging or condemning — and the giving in view is the whole disposition of generosity, mercy, and forbearance, not a deposit made with expectation of yield. The immediately preceding clause is with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again, which is the principle in both its directions. To extract the promise and drop the context turns a call to open-handed mercy into a scheme for personal increase, and it makes God a party to the very calculation the passage was given to abolish.

The other half of the corruption is the quiet exemption we grant ourselves under Mat 7:2. The saying is almost universally quoted as a prohibition of any moral assessment whatever — which the same chapter refutes, since a few verses later the disciples are told to beware of false prophets and to know them by their fruits, a judgment that requires discernment. What is forbidden is the judgment of the man with a beam in his own eye: censoriousness that applies a strict standard outward and a lenient one inward. The principle to recover is that the standard is reflexive. A man who wants mercy must extend it; a man who deals in suspicion will be dealt with in suspicion; and the God who measured the waters in the hollow of his hand (Isa 40:12) is not going to be short of accuracy when He applies a man's own rule to him.
roots_summary: Hebrew middâh is a measure or extent, from mādad, to measure; 'ēphâh and hin are the dry and liquid standards the law requires to be just. Greek metron is a measure, and metreō the verb to mete.
roots_lines: Hebrew middâh (H4060) — measure, extent, stature; from mādad, to measure or stretch out.
Hebrew 'ēphâh (H374) — the standard dry measure; ye shall have just balances, a just ephah, and a just hin (Lev 19:36).
Hebrew 'eben w''eben — a stone and a stone, the idiom for divers weights; a false balance is abomination to the LORD (Pro 11:1).
Greek metron (G3358) — a measure or portion; the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ (Eph 4:13).
Greek metreō (G3354) — to measure or mete out; with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again (Mat 7:2).
usage: Of God as measurer of creation: who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand (Isa 40:12).
Of the reflexive standard: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again (Mat 7:2).
Of the Spirit given to Christ without limit: God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him (Joh 3:34).

Matthew 7:2

pos: n. (rendering Hebrew netach and keseph in idiom, Greek drachmē and argurion)
etymology: From Old French piece, a fragment or portion. In the King James the word most often appears in the phrase pieces of silver, where the Hebrew or Greek names only the metal and the word pieces is supplied by the translators — thirty of silver being thirty shekels' weight. The word therefore carries in Scripture an association with price and with betrayal that its plain sense would not suggest.
biblical_def: The most famous pieces in Scripture are thirty of silver, and the prophecy came first. Zechariah, playing the part of a shepherd dismissed by the flock, asks his wages and receives the price of a gored slave: “And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver” (Zec 11:12). Centuries later a disciple names his own figure for the same Shepherd: “What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver” (Mat 26:15). The valuation of Christ by those who sold Him is one of the most exact fulfilments in the Bible, down to the potter's field the money bought. Against that stands a piece of silver of an entirely different kind — one coin out of ten, lost in a house, and the trouble taken to find it: “Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?” (Luk 15:8). The parable is about the value God places on one sinner, and its force is that the coin is worth the candle, the broom, and the whole evening. The word also appears in the Lord's warning about patching: “No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto an old garment, for that which is put in to fill it up taketh from the garment, and the rent is made worse” (Mat 9:16) — the gospel is not a patch for an old religion, and attempts to sew it on tear both.
webster_summary: A fragment or part of anything; a separate portion; a coin — whence the thirty pieces of silver for which Christ was sold, the lost piece the woman swept the house to find, and the piece of new cloth that must not be sewn on an old garment.
webster_full: PIECE, n. 1. A fragment or part of any thing separated from the whole, in any manner.
2. A part of any thing, though not separated, or separated only in idea; as a piece of excellent workmanship.
3. A separate portion of any kind; a distinct thing; as a piece of land, a piece of money.
4. A coin; as a piece of silver, a piece of eight.
5. In Scripture, thirty pieces of silver. Zech. 11; Matt. 26. Ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece. Luke 15.
corruption_summary: Christianity is treated as a patch to be sewn onto an existing life or an existing religion, improving it here and there, when the Lord Jesus explicitly denies that His gospel can be added to an old garment without tearing both.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 9:16 is a warning against exactly the arrangement most people want: to keep the garment they have and mend it with a piece of Christ. The Lord says the repair fails and makes the rent worse, and He says it in answer to a question about whether His disciples should keep the old fasts. His point is not that the old covenant was worthless but that what He brings is not an improvement to a system — it is a new garment, and a new birth. The corruption appears wherever conversion is presented as the addition of religious observance to an otherwise unchanged life, or as the tidying of a moral record. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away. The patch theory produces the miserable condition of a man who has enough religion to spoil his sin and not enough to displace it.

The second corruption concerns valuation. Judas set a price of thirty pieces on the Son of God, and Scripture is careful to record that this was the compensation fixed in the law for a slave gored by an ox — the cheapest human valuation the statute knew. Men still price Christ, and the sums are usually smaller: a position, a relationship, a habit, a reputation. Set against that is the woman's search for one coin (Luk 15:8), which teaches the opposite valuation — what heaven thinks a single sinner is worth. The principle to recover is that both prices are on record: what men will take for Christ, and what God will spend for a man. Ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew netach is a piece of a divided sacrifice; the phrase rendered pieces of silver names only keseph, silver, the weight being understood. Greek drachmē is a silver coin of about a day's wage, and argurion a piece of silver.
roots_lines: Hebrew keseph (H3701) — silver, and hence money; thirty of silver (Zec 11:12), the word pieces being supplied by the translators.
Hebrew netach (H5409) — a piece of a divided animal; the burnt offering cut into his pieces (Lev 1:6).
Greek drachmē (G1406) — a Greek silver coin worth about a day's wage; the ten pieces of silver of Luk 15:8.
Greek argurion (G694) — silver, a piece of silver; thirty pieces of silver (Mat 26:15), and the money cast down in the temple.
Hebrew sh'lōshīm keseph — thirty of silver; the compensation fixed in Exo 21:32 for a servant gored by an ox, and so the price of a slave.
usage: Of the price prophesied: so they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver (Zec 11:12).
Of the price paid: they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver (Mat 26:15).
Of the one coin sought: if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently (Luk 15:8).

pos: n. pl. (rendering Hebrew beged and simlah, Greek himation and sparganon)
etymology: From Old English clath, cloth. The Hebrew beged is the general word for a garment, and it comes from a root meaning to act treacherously or cover over — the same consonants giving both garment and deal falsely, since a covering may conceal as well as clothe. Scripture exploits the ambiguity: clothes both dignify and disguise, and the rending of them is the standard sign that what was hidden has come out.
biblical_def: Clothes in Scripture mark the great transitions of a life, and they are placed at the two ends of the Lord's own. At the beginning: “And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luk 2:7) — the swaddling bands being the ordinary wrapping of any poor child, and the appointed sign given to the shepherds, so that the mark of the Messiah was that He looked like anyone else. At the other end, and at a graveside not His own: “And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go” (Joh 11:44) — Lazarus is raised but still bound, and the church is given the office of unbinding what Christ has made alive. The tearing of clothes is Scripture's standard sign of grief or of horror, and it is at the trial that the gesture becomes a self-condemnation: “Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses?” (Mat 26:65) — the law forbade the high priest to rend his garments, and in tearing them to condemn the true High Priest he ended his own office by the act. Joel warns against the gesture without the substance: rend your heart, and not your garments. Clothing is finally the Bible's picture of righteousness, from the coats of skins in Eden to the fine linen which is the righteousness of saints.
webster_summary: Garments; the covering of the body; and in Scripture the swaddling clothes of the infant Christ, the graveclothes Lazarus was loosed from, the clothes rent in grief or in judgment, and the raiment which figures righteousness given or lacked.
webster_full: CLOTHES, n. plural of cloth. 1. Garments for the human body; dress; vestments; vesture.
2. The covering of a bed; bed clothes.
3. In Hebrew, a garment; from a root which also signifies to cover over or deal treacherously, a covering serving to conceal as well as to clothe.
4. To rend the clothes, an ancient token of grief, indignation, or horror. Gen. 37; Matt. 26.
5. In Scripture, wrapped him in swaddling clothes. Luke 2. Bound hand and foot with graveclothes. John 11.
corruption_summary: Outward religious gesture is substituted for inward repentance, so that the rending of garments continues while the heart is untouched — the very exchange Joel names and the high priest performed at the trial of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Joel's command — rend your heart, and not your garments — identifies the oldest substitution in religion: the visible act standing in for the invisible change. The gesture is not condemned in itself; tearing the clothes was a genuine expression of grief, and Scripture records it of Jacob, David, Job, and Paul without rebuke. What is condemned is the gesture performed instead of repentance, and its modern forms are numerous and respectable: the public apology carefully worded to concede nothing, the emotional response at a meeting that changes no habit, the season of religious observance that leaves the besetting sin exactly where it was. God's stated preference is not for less feeling but for more reality: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.

Mat 26:65 is the most terrible instance in Scripture, and its detail rewards attention. The law expressly forbade the high priest to rend his clothes, on pain of death; in tearing them to pronounce the true High Priest a blasphemer, Caiaphas performed the outward sign of horror at blasphemy while committing it, and by the act publicly ended the office he was defending. The principle to recover is the one Lazarus's graveclothes illustrate from the other side (Joh 11:44): what Christ makes alive He also intends to be unbound, and the church's work with a raised man is to loose him and let him go — not to leave him in the wrappings of a life he has been brought out of. Religion that only tears cloth leaves the man exactly as he was; the gospel raises him and then takes the bandages off.
roots_summary: Hebrew beged is a garment, from a root meaning to cover over or deal treacherously; simlah is an outer wrapper or mantle. Greek himation is an outer garment, sparganon a swaddling band, and keiria the graveclothes of Lazarus.
roots_lines: Hebrew beged (H899) — a garment or covering; from bāgad, to cover over, and so to act treacherously, a covering that may conceal.
Hebrew simlah (H8071) — a mantle or outer wrapper; the garment taken in pledge which must be returned before sundown (Exo 22:26).
Hebrew qāra' b'gādīm — to rend the garments; the standard sign of mourning or horror, forbidden to the high priest (Lev 21:10).
Greek sparganon — a swaddling band; whence sparganoo, to wrap in swaddling clothes (Luk 2:7), the ordinary wrapping of an infant.
Greek keiria (G2750) — a winding sheet or bandage; bound hand and foot with graveclothes (Joh 11:44).
usage: Of the sign given to the shepherds: wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger (Luk 2:7).
Of the raised man still bound: bound hand and foot with graveclothes... Loose him, and let him go (Joh 11:44).
Of the gesture that condemned its maker: then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy (Mat 26:65).

etymology: From Old French vaissel, from Latin vascellum, a small vase. The Hebrew k'lī is far broader than the English — it means any implement, utensil, weapon, or article whatever, anything made for a use — and that is the sense Scripture presses. A vessel is defined by the purpose it was formed to serve and by the hand that formed it, which is why the potter and the clay are never far from the word.
biblical_def: A vessel in Scripture is a made thing with a use, and the doctrine attached to it is that the Maker assigns the use. Paul states the sovereign right in the plainest terms: “Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?” (Rom 9:21) — of the same lump being the crux, since the clay is not of two qualities and the distinction rests wholly in the potter's purpose. Yet the same apostle sets alongside that sovereignty a genuine responsibility, and the two stand together without apology: “If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work” (2Ti 2:21). The vessel is also deliberately unimpressive, and Paul explains why the treasure is put in such poor containers: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7) — common baked clay, cheap and breakable, chosen so that no one mistakes the source of the power. And the word governs one of the New Testament's central instructions to husbands, where weaker is a statement about relative strength and emphatically not about worth, since the same sentence makes them joint heirs: “ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered” (1Pe 3:7). The sanction is remarkable — a man's treatment of his wife can obstruct his prayers.
webster_summary: A utensil for holding something; any implement or article made for a use; and in Scripture the vessel formed by the potter unto honour or dishonour, the earthen vessel holding the treasure, and the wife honoured as the weaker vessel and joint heir.
webster_full: VESSEL, n. 1. A cask or utensil proper for holding liquors and other things, as a tub, pipe, puncheon, bottle or dish.
2. Any building used in navigation; a ship, brig, sloop or the like.
3. In anatomy, a tube or canal in which the blood and other humors are contained and circulated.
4. In Hebrew, any implement, utensil, weapon or article whatever; that which is made for a use.
5. In Scripture, a chosen vessel unto me. Acts 9. This treasure in earthen vessels. 2 Cor. 4. The weaker vessel. 1 Pet. 3.
corruption_summary: The description of the wife as the weaker vessel is read as a statement of lesser worth or competence, when the same verse makes her a joint heir and makes a husband's failure here a hindrance to his prayers.
corruption_paragraphs: 1Pe 3:7 has been misused in both directions. Some have taken weaker vessel as a verdict on a woman's worth, capacity, or spiritual standing, and used it to justify condescension or worse. The verse itself forbids the reading twice over: the husband is commanded to give honour, and the reason given is that they are heirs together of the grace of life — equal inheritors of the same salvation. The comparison is one of relative physical strength and of the protection that follows from it, and the whole thrust of the instruction is the opposite of licence: greater strength imposes greater duty, exactly as the shepherd's strength exists for the flock. The sanction attached is unique in the New Testament — that your prayers be not hindered — which means a man's standing at the throne of grace is affected by how he treats his wife at home.

The opposite corruption denies any creational difference at all, treating the passage as a cultural relic to be discarded and with it the whole structure of male responsibility it establishes. Scripture's order is not a ranking of value but an assignment of duty: husbands love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it. Remove the order and the duty goes with it, and what replaces it is not equality but the absence of anyone obliged to lay his life down. The principle to recover joins both halves of the verse: distinct in strength and calling, equal as heirs together of the grace of life — and both truths held by a man who remembers that he is himself only an earthen vessel (2Co 4:7), holding a treasure he did not make and cannot account for.
roots_summary: Hebrew k'lī is any implement, utensil, weapon, or article made for a use; yotser is the potter, from yātsar, to form. Greek skeuos is a vessel, implement, or instrument, and ostrakinos means made of baked clay.
roots_lines: Hebrew k'lī (H3627) — a vessel, implement, utensil, or weapon; anything prepared for a use, including the vessels of the sanctuary.
Hebrew yātsar (H3335) — to form or fashion as a potter; the verb used of God forming man of the dust (Gen 2:7) and of the potter at his wheel (Jer 18:4).
Greek skeuos (G4632) — a vessel, implement, or instrument; a chosen vessel unto me (Act 9:15), and the weaker vessel (1Pe 3:7).
Greek ostrakinos (G3749) — made of baked clay, earthen; this treasure in earthen vessels (2Co 4:7), common and breakable.
Greek kerameus (G2763) — a potter; hath not the potter power over the clay (Rom 9:21).
usage: Of the potter's right: of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour (Rom 9:21).
Of the treasure and its container: we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God (2Co 4:7).
Of the wife honoured as joint heir: giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life (1Pe 3:7).

etymology: From Old English wudu. The Hebrew 'ēts means both a living tree and cut timber — the same word serving for the tree of life and for the wood of the burnt offering — and the Greek xulon does the same, which is why the New Testament can say Christ bore our sins on the tree, using the word for a piece of timber. The single word joining living tree and dead wood carries a good deal of biblical theology on its back.
biblical_def: Wood in Scripture runs from the ark to the cross, and its most affecting appearance is on the shoulders of a son: “And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son; and he took the fire in his hand, and a knife; and they went both of them together” (Gen 22:6). The son carries the wood on which he is to be offered up the hill, while the father carries the fire and the knife — a scene the church has never been able to read without seeing another Son and another hill. Wood is also the material God specifies for the vessels of His presence, overlaid but not replaced: “they shall make an ark of shittim wood: two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof” (Exo 25:10) — acacia, a desert timber, gold without and within, the humble substance and the glory joined in one object. Wood marks servitude in the covenant with the Gibeonites, whose deception is answered with mercy and a permanent office: “Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation” (Jos 9:21) — they lied to survive, and were made servants of the sanctuary rather than corpses. And Paul uses wood as one of the perishable materials a man may build with on the one foundation: “Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble” (1Co 3:12) — the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire, and the wood will not survive the testing though the builder may.
webster_summary: The hard substance of trees; timber; and in Scripture the wood of the burnt offering laid on Isaac, the shittim wood of the ark overlaid with gold, the hewers of wood among the congregation, and the perishable material some build with on the one foundation.
webster_full: WOOD, n. 1. A large and thick collection of trees; a forest.
2. The substance of trees; the hard fibrous substance which composes the body of a tree and its branches.
3. Timber; wood cut and prepared for use in building or burning.
4. In Hebrew and Greek alike, the same word serves for a living tree and for cut timber; whence Christ bare our sins in his own body on the tree. 1 Pet. 2.
5. In Scripture, Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son. Gen. 22.
corruption_summary: The binding of Isaac is charged against God as divine cruelty, and its typological direction is missed — that the Father did not spare His own Son, and that the ram caught in the thicket is the whole doctrine of substitution in a single image.
corruption_paragraphs: Gen 22 is regularly presented as the Bible's moral scandal: a God who commands child sacrifice, however He relents. The reading ignores what the narrative itself insists on. God expressly forbids child sacrifice everywhere in the law, calling it an abomination He never commanded nor spoke, neither came it into His mind; the text states in advance that this was a testing; and the outcome is not a death but a provision — God will provide himself a lamb, and a ram is found caught in a thicket. The whole episode is designed to teach substitution: the son carries the wood up the hill, the knife is raised, and another dies in his place. Abraham names the mountain Jehovah-jireh, and the narrator adds that in the mount of the LORD it shall be seen — a location later occupied by the temple, and by a crucifixion.

The deeper point is what the story shows about God rather than about Abraham. Paul says it plainly: he that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. What Abraham was stopped from doing, God did. There was no substitute for the Substitute, no ram in the thicket at Calvary, and no voice from heaven halting the knife. The principle to recover is that the wood is one wood throughout Scripture — the timber laid on Isaac's shoulders, the shittim wood of the ark of the covenant, and the tree on which Christ bore our sins in his own body. Wood is also what will not survive the fire when a man's work is tried (1Co 3:12), which is a warning to build on the one foundation with something better.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ēts means both tree and timber; shittīm is the acacia of the desert, the wood of the tabernacle furniture. Greek xulon likewise means wood, timber, or tree, and is the New Testament's word for the cross.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ēts (H6086) — tree, wood, timber; the tree of life and the wood of the burnt offering are the same noun.
Hebrew shittīm (H7848) — shittim or acacia wood, the durable desert timber of the ark, table, and altar (Exo 25:10).
Hebrew chōt'bē 'ētsīm — hewers of wood; the office assigned to the Gibeonites in the service of the congregation (Jos 9:21).
Greek xulon (G3586) — wood, timber, or tree; who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree (1Pe 2:24).
Greek stauros (G4716) — a cross or upright stake; the instrument on which Christ was crucified, called xulon where the curse of Deu 21:23 is in view.
usage: Of the son carrying the wood: Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son (Gen 22:6).
Of the material of the sanctuary: they shall make an ark of shittim wood (Exo 25:10).
Of perishable building: if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble (1Co 3:12).
scriptures: Genesis 22:6
